nameStory: Coast cinquefoil gets its name from its preferred seaside habitat along rocky shores and sandy beaches. The word 'cinquefoil' comes from the French 'cinq feuilles' meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's characteristic five-leaflet pattern that most species in this group share.
description: Coast cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial plant that hugs the ground in coastal areas of New England. This hardy little member of the rose family forms spreading mats rarely more than 6 inches tall, with woody stems that creep along the ground. Its small yellow flowers bloom throughout the summer, each with five rounded petals typical of the rose family. The plant's compact, cushion-like growth helps it survive the harsh winds and salt spray of ocean environments.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, low mats that spread horizontally along the ground, with woody stems that feel sturdy despite being only a few inches tall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers about half an inch across with five rounded petals and a cluster of yellow stamens in the center, appearing from June through September

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small compound leaves typically divided into 3-5 wedge-shaped leaflets that feel somewhat thick and waxy, often with a silvery-green appearance

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Found exclusively in coastal environments within just a few hundred yards of salt water, growing in sandy soil or rocky crevices

habitat: Coast cinquefoil is found only in immediate coastal areas of New England, particularly along rocky shores, sandy beaches, and coastal dunes. It thrives in well-drained, often sandy soils that can tolerate salt spray and harsh ocean winds. Look for it growing alongside other salt-tolerant plants like beach pea and seaside goldenrod in Massachusetts, where it's extremely rare.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, silvery-green leaflets unfurling from woody stems. The plant begins to green up and spread its mat-like growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers appearing continuously from June through September. This is the best time for identification when flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, and leaves often take on reddish tints. Seeds develop in small, dry clusters.
seasonality.winter: Woody stems persist above ground, and some leaves may remain evergreen in protected coastal locations, appearing bronze or reddish.

funFact: Coast cinquefoil is so rare in New England that it has been documented at only one location in recent decades, making it one of the region's rarest native plants and a true botanical treasure for anyone lucky enough to spot it!
confusionNotes: Coast cinquefoil might be confused with other low-growing coastal plants, but its five-petaled yellow flowers and compound leaves with 3-5 leaflets distinguish it from most seaside vegetation. Remember: if it's not within sight of the ocean, it's definitely not coast cinquefoil!
contextualKnowledge: **Note: Information about this extremely rare species is limited and some details should be verified with current botanical sources.** Coast cinquefoil's rarity in New England makes it a species of conservation concern, and any sightings should be reported to local botanists or conservation organizations.
compareHints: Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves. While common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have similar yellow flowers, they grow in woodlands and fields rather than coastal areas, and lack the dense, cushion-like growth habit that helps coast cinquefoil survive ocean storms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
